newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinians reject U.S. peace compromise.
newsitem.headline: Palestinians reject U.S. peace compromise.

text.p: The PLO has rejected a U.S. proposal aimed at resolving the one issue holding up Israel's handover of most of the West Bank town of Hebron to Palestinian self-rule, a PLO official said on Thursday.

Tayeb Abdel-Rahim, general secretary of the Palestinian presidency, said the U.S. proposal -- for Israel to hand over most of the West Bank by mid-1998 -- violated peace accords calling for that pullout by September of this year.

U.S. Middle East peace envoy Dennis Ross is struggling to save a deal on Hebron. But both sides admit the sticking point has less to do with Hebron than with three further transfers of West Bank areas to Palestinian control.

"Israel has proposed to end the last stage of further redeployments from the rest of the West Bank in 1999. We rejected that, so to break the deadlock in the talks, Ross proposed as a compromise mid-1998, and we rejected this as well," Abdel-Rahim told Reuters.

"The Palestinian leadership will not make and cannot make any more compromises, especially on dates agreed in the original deal and the U.S. compromise is a violation of the deal that was signed by U.S. President Bill Clinton," he said.

PLO-Israeli talks over an Israeli pullout from 80 percent of Hebron have been deadlocked over the PLO's insistence that Israel adhere to a 1995 interim peace deal which stated that Israel would complete the other handovers 18 months after the inauguration of the Palestinian Legislative Council.
The council was inaugurated on March 7, 1996, meaning the handovers would have to be completed by September 7, 1997.

The Arab world views an agreement to give Palestinians self-rule in the volatile town as a test of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's commitment to the peace deals he inherited from the ousted Labour government last May.
Netanyahu wants to link the last handover to talks due to be completed by May 1999 on the future of Jewish settlers.

"Giving us new dates means there is a new reference to the peace process other than the signed accords, and therefore we can't trust that the U.S. will adhere to its new commitments and neither will Israel since they have both abandoned signed deals," Abdel-Rahim said.
Palestinians hope ultimately to establish a state on the West Bank and Gaza Strip -- a goal opposed by Netanyahu.

"Israel is still insisting on reopening and changing signed deals, and when they say they want to change agreed dates, we look with astonishment at their statements that they are committed to the accords," Abdel-Rahim said. "We have no confidence that they would respect their new commitments."

"Although we are asking the U.S. to continue playing a role in the peace process along with Egypt and other parties, we are also asking the U.S. to adhere to deals it signed and to respect agreed dates," Abdel-Rahim said.
Some 400 Jews live and study in the heart of Hebron surrounded by 100,000 Arabs. The town, a flashpoint of violence, is holy to Jews and Moslems as the burial place of the biblical Abraham.
